summary: Provides a collection of additional matching rules for LDAP. They are simple adaptations of matching rules defined for the X.500 Directory, and most are already in wide use. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: When you search a directory, a matching rule decides whether the text you typed counts as the same as the value stored in the directory. LDAP already had a few of these rules. RFC 3698 adds twelve more, taken from the older X.500 directory standard, and gives each one a name, a number and the kind of value it works on.

questions: which rfc replaced rfc 2798 matching rule descriptions
subtitle: Twelve more ways for an LDAP directory to decide that two values match, borrowed from X.500.

tldr.problem: LDAP directories need rules that say when a search value matches a stored value, and several rules already used with X.500 directories were not yet written down for LDAP.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adapts twelve X.500 matching rules for LDAP, giving each one a plain description, an object identifier (OID) and the attribute syntax it applies to.
tldr.outcome: Most of the rules were already in wide use, for example with the inetOrgPerson and Policy Core schemas. The text replaces the matching rule descriptions in RFC 2798, and RFC 4517 later updated this RFC.

today: RFC 3698 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2004 and is listed as updated by RFC 4517. It updates RFC 2798, taking over that RFC's matching rule descriptions.

sections.title: Background and Intended Use
sections.content:
The document adapts additional X.500 Directory matching rules for use with the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol. Most of these rules are widely used today on the Internet, such as in support of the inetOrgPerson and Policy Core Information Model LDAP schemas. The rules are applicable to many other applications.

The document supersedes the informational matching rules descriptions provided in RFC 2798 that are now provided here. Specifically, section 2 of this document replaces section 9.3.3 of RFC 2798.

Schema definitions are provided using LDAP description formats. Definitions provided here are formatted, and line wrapped, for readability.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules in this document come from the X.500 directory standard, which predates LDAP and was designed for a much larger directory system. Most of them are already in wide use on the Internet, for example in the schema for organisation entries and in the schema for network policy.

sections.title: The Matching Rules
sections.content:
Each matching rule is given a name, an object identifier and the attribute syntax it applies to. The object identifiers all sit in the arc 2.5.13, which was already assigned to the X.500 matching rules, so this document makes no new OID assignments. It only associates LDAP matching rule descriptions with existing X.500 matching rules.

Twelve rules are defined. booleanMatch compares an asserted Boolean value with an attribute value of BOOLEAN syntax. caseExactMatch compares for equality an asserted value with an attribute value of DirectoryString syntax, ignoring nothing, so it differs from caseIgnoreMatch only in that case is not ignored. caseExactOrderingMatch compares collation order, again without folding letters. caseExactSubstringsMatch determines whether the asserted values are substrings of an attribute value of DirectoryString syntax. caseIgnoreListSubstringsMatch compares an asserted substring with an attribute value that is a sequence of DirectoryStrings, where case is not significant.

The remaining rules are directoryStringFirstComponentMatch, integerOrderingMatch, keywordMatch, numericStringOrderingMatch, octetStringOrderingMatch, storedPrefixMatch and wordMatch. Every one of them is defined in the same way: a name, an object identifier and a SYNTAX line giving the attribute syntax the rule applies to.
sections.plainLanguage: Each rule has a name, a number and the kind of value it works on. The numbers all come from the arc 2.5.13, which X.500 already owned, so this document adds no new numbers to the registry. It only describes rules that already exist in a form LDAP can use.

sections.title: What Each Rule Does
sections.content:
The equality and ordering rules are straightforward. booleanMatch returns TRUE if and only if the asserted Boolean and the stored Boolean are the same, that is, both TRUE or both FALSE. caseExactMatch is identical to caseIgnoreMatch except that case is not ignored. caseExactOrderingMatch is identical to caseIgnoreOrderingMatch except that letters are not folded. integerOrderingMatch compares the ordering of an asserted integer with an attribute value of INTEGER syntax and returns True if the attribute value is less than the asserted value. numericStringOrderingMatch compares collation order with a NumericString attribute value, skipping all space characters during comparison, since case is irrelevant as the characters are numeric. octetStringOrderingMatch compares octet strings from the first octet to the last and from the most significant bit to the least significant bit within an octet; the first occurrence of a different bit determines the ordering, a zero bit precedes a one bit, and if the strings are identical but have different numbers of octets, the shorter string precedes the longer one.

The substring and word rules work on parts of a value. caseExactSubstringsMatch determines whether the asserted values are substrings of a DirectoryString attribute value, with case not ignored. caseIgnoreListSubstringsMatch compares an asserted substring with an attribute value that is a sequence of DirectoryStrings, and the asserted value matches if it matches the string formed by concatenating the stored strings; no initial, any or final value of the asserted value is considered to match a substring that spans more than one of the stored strings. directoryStringFirstComponentMatch compares an asserted DirectoryString with an attribute value of type SEQUENCE whose first component is mandatory and of type DirectoryString, returning TRUE if the first component matches by the rules of caseIgnoreMatch. keywordMatch compares an asserted string with keywords in a DirectoryString attribute value and returns TRUE if the asserted value matches any keyword, though the identification of keywords and the exactness of the match are both implementation specific. storedPrefixMatch determines whether a DirectoryString attribute value is a prefix of the asserted value, without regard to case; the document notes it can be used to compare telephone area codes in the directory with a purported telephone number. wordMatch compares an asserted string with words in a DirectoryString attribute value, where individual word matching is as for caseIgnoreMatch and the precise definition of a word is implementation specific.
sections.plainLanguage: Some rules ask whether two values are equal, some ask which comes first, and some look inside a value for a piece. A few details are left to the implementation, such as what counts as a word and how keywords are spotted in a value.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The general LDAP security considerations are applicable to the use of this schema. Additional considerations are noted above where appropriate.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing here changes the general rules for securing an LDAP directory. The usual LDAP security advice applies.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The Internet Assigned Numbers Authority has updated the LDAP descriptors registry as indicated in the template. The template names the contact for further information as Kurt Zeilenga, gives the specification as RFC 3698, and names the IESG as the author or change controller.

Twelve descriptors have been added, each of type M, which stands for Matching Rule: booleanMatch at 2.5.13.13, caseExactMatch at 2.5.13.5, caseExactOrderingMatch at 2.5.13.6, caseExactSubstringsMatch at 2.5.13.7, caseIgnoreListSubstringsMatch at 2.5.13.12, directoryStringFirstComponentMatch at 2.5.13.31, integerOrderingMatch at 2.5.13.15, keywordMatch at 2.5.13.33, numericStringOrderingMatch at 2.5.13.9, octetStringOrderingMatch at 2.5.13.18, storedPrefixMatch at 2.5.13.41 and wordMatch at 2.5.13.32.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA's list of LDAP descriptors now names all twelve rules and gives each one its number. The document adds no new numbers; it only points the LDAP names at the X.500 ones that already existed.
